passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 pm. I keep thinking how it started. Month-end, and the delivery count was a few short. I rounded it up so the team wouldn’t get a red flag. Deepika, our lead, said, “Everyone does it. It protects us.”
Last month I skipped the incident note because it “would only stir things.” This month it took me half a minute to round the number, and I didn’t feel much.
Tonight I noticed the difference. The first time my stomach flipped for two days. Now I say “everyone does it” too, exactly like Deepika. I’m not proud of that.
— Vikas

qa.q: Who told Vikas that everyone does it?
qa.a: Deepika, the lead, told Vikas that everyone does it and that it protects the team.

qa.q: How did Vikas's feeling about rounding the number change over the months?
qa.a: The first time Vikas's stomach flipped for two days, but now it takes half a minute and Vikas hardly feels anything. The guilt has been quieted by repeating that everyone does it.

qa.q: What turning point did Vikas reach that night?
qa.a: Vikas noticed the change in how easy it had become and that the same excuse was being used. That noticing is the point where Vikas could choose to stop.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen the rounding of numbers?
qa.a: Deepika seems to see it as a way of protecting the team from red flags, and likely believes it is harmless. Saying everyone does it helps make it feel normal.

grounding: Shows a person joining a small concealment step by step, quieting guilt with the belief that everyone does it and it protects the team.

passage:
Tenzin: Did you file the missed maintenance report?
Chetan: Not yet. It’s one late check. Nothing happened.
Tenzin: You skipped one last month too.
Chetan: That was different. We were slammed.
Tenzin: Who else knows the check was late?
Chetan: Only you. Nobody asked.
Tenzin: And the number on Friday’s slide?
Chetan: I rounded it. Everyone does it. It keeps the team out of trouble.
Tenzin: Hmm.
Chetan: I know how that sounds. It’s getting easier each time. That’s what worries me.
Tenzin: Then maybe file the report today.
Chetan: Maybe. Ask me after lunch.

qa.q: What did Chetan say about the number on Friday's slide?
qa.a: Chetan said it was rounded and that everyone does it to keep the team out of trouble.

qa.q: What is Chetan worried about when saying it is getting easier?
qa.a: Chetan is uneasy that each small concealment makes the next one simpler. Chetan says that is exactly the worry, so the guilt is still there.

qa.q: What would be a good next step for Chetan, based on the chat?
qa.a: Filing the missed report today, as Tenzin suggests, would stop the chain before another skipped check. The delay to after lunch shows Chetan is still tempted to put it off.

qa.q: How might Tenzin be feeling during this exchange?
qa.a: Tenzin seems concerned but gentle, asking questions rather than accusing. Suggesting filing the report today shows Tenzin wants to help Chetan.

grounding: Shows a person sliding into covering up, with a missed report and a rounded figure, calming guilt with everyone does it.

passage: The first time, it was only one number. Ramesh's Bengaluru sales team was short of target by two orders, and his manager, Yogesh, said, 'Book the March orders in February. Everyone does it. It keeps us all safe.' Ramesh felt a small, cold knot in his stomach, but he did it. The next month it was five orders. The knot was smaller. By June he was the one showing the new joiner how to move dates in the system. 'Relax,' he told her, hearing Yogesh's voice in his own. 'It keeps us all safe.' That night, lying awake, he realised he couldn't remember when he'd stopped feeling the knot.

qa.q: How many orders was the team short by the first time?
qa.a: Two orders.

qa.q: What happened to Ramesh's guilt over the months?
qa.a: It shrank; the cold knot got smaller each month until he couldn't remember when he'd stopped feeling it.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do now that he has noticed?
qa.a: Stop moving dates, tell the new joiner honestly that it was wrong, and raise the practice with someone above Yogesh or through the company's ethics channel.

qa.q: How might the new joiner see what Ramesh taught her?
qa.a: She may accept it as normal, since a senior told her it keeps everyone safe, and begin the same slide.

grounding: An employee joins a small fudge of numbers, and each step makes the next easier as guilt is quieted by team excuses.

passage:
'Just sign the calibration sheet,' Lokesh said, not looking up. 'We'll do the check tomorrow.'
Shalini held the pen. 'You said that last week.'
'And nothing happened, right? The machine's fine.'
'We signed it as done on the fourteenth. It wasn't.'
'Everyone signs it. The audit only looks for signatures.' He finally looked at her. 'You want the whole lab in trouble for one missed check?'
She signed. Her hand felt heavy.
The next Friday, Lokesh didn't even ask. He just left the sheet on her bench with a sticky note: 'Usual.'
Shalini stared at it. 'Usual,' she said aloud. Three weeks ago she'd never have signed. Now there was a 'usual'.
She peeled off the note and went to find the calibration kit.

qa.q: What did Lokesh's sticky note say?
qa.a: 'Usual.'

qa.q: What does Shalini's heavy hand when signing suggest?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing she was signing for a check that hadn't happened.

qa.q: What did Shalini do at the end, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She went to find the calibration kit and do the check, breaking the slide before it became normal.

qa.q: How does Lokesh seem to see the skipped checks?
qa.a: As harmless paperwork, telling himself the audit only looks for signatures and that it protects the lab.

grounding: A lab worker signs one false check under pressure, notices how quickly it became 'usual', and stops the slide.

passage: At the warehouse, our team got a bonus for every month with 'zero incidents'. The first near-miss I didn't report was small: a pallet slipped off the forklift and missed Pallavi's foot by a hand's width. Our supervisor said, 'Nobody's hurt. Don't spoil the record for the whole team.' I told myself he was right. The second time a shelf wobbled, I said nothing without even being asked. By the fourth, I was the one telling new people, 'We sort these things ourselves.' Then Pallavi fractured her wrist when that same shelf finally came down. She reported everything, including the earlier near-misses, and the shelves were all checked that week. I'm Vishal, and I still can't forgive myself for how easy each silence got.

qa.q: What was the team's bonus for?
qa.a: Every month with 'zero incidents'.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel looking back?
qa.a: Vishal feels deep guilt and regret, unable to forgive how easy each silence became.

qa.q: What could Vishal have done at the first near-miss?
qa.a: Reported it despite the supervisor's words, so the shelf could have been checked before anyone was hurt.

qa.q: What was it like for Pallavi to report everything after her injury?
qa.a: Painful and probably lonely, going against the team's record, but necessary to stop further harm.

grounding: A worker's small silence about a near-miss grows into a habit of covering up, each step easier, until someone is hurt.

passage:
Supervisor's note, quality lab, Friday.
Today Pema, 25, came to my desk and asked to speak privately. For four months, she said, the cold-room temperature logs had been "tidied". It began in February, when the logger failed one night and Noor, the senior technician, filled in the missing readings from memory. "Everyone does it," Noor told her. "It protects the team." The next week Pema copied one reading. Then a whole night. By May she was writing numbers without looking at the gauge. She said the guilt got quieter each time, and that frightened her more than the guilt. She was pale and kept apologising. I thanked her for coming and said I would deal with the logs and the process, not her character. Next: this afternoon I pulled the affected batches for testing, informed the plant head in writing, and asked for a meeting with Noor and HR on Monday.

qa.q: When did the tidying of the temperature logs begin?
qa.a: It began in February, when the logger failed one night.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as the guilt grew quieter?
qa.a: Pema was frightened that the guilt got quieter each time, even more than by the guilt itself.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do next, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The supervisor pulled the affected batches for testing, informed the plant head in writing and set a meeting, which protects people and fixes the process.

qa.q: How might Noor see the tidying that started it all?
qa.a: Noor seems to see it as harmless team protection, saying "everyone does it", without facing how each step made the next easier.

grounding: The supervisor's note shows Pema sliding step by step into a cover-up, each fudged reading easier than the last, until she speaks up.
